Conservatives and Labour fail to get a grip on foreigners’ unpaid NHS bills

Years of warnings. Hundreds of millions written off. British employers handed higher taxes while patients wait for care.

Steve English · 21 October 2026 · England-focused investigation
Read articleFigures & methodologySourcesPolicy library

The Conservatives had years to get a grip on unpaid overseas-patient bills. Labour inherited the collection failures and now owes the public answers about what it is doing to fix them.

Across the financial years verified for this investigation between 2010/11 and 2024/25, NHS providers in England recorded approximately £409 million in overseas-patient losses and write-offs.

That excludes 2012/13, which remains unverified here. These figures cover chargeable overseas-patient treatment generally, rather than maternity alone. [1][2][3][4][5][6]

Hundreds of millions written off. Warnings stretching back more than a decade. Politicians repeatedly telling us the NHS needs more money.

Before asking taxpayers to dig deeper, how about collecting the money hospitals are already owed?

Ministers had evidence that hospitals were missing chargeable patients, struggling to collect payments and writing off debts. The weaknesses were studied, published and discussed.

The bills kept coming.

The Conservatives knew

In October 2013, the Department of Health published research identifying weaknesses in the overseas charging system.

Staff acknowledged that chargeable patients escaped identification. Even proactive trusts admitted they were missing people who should have been billed. Researchers found inconsistent approaches between hospitals and substantial scope to improve identification and recovery. [8][9]

Conservative ministers had years to respond.

By 2016, the National Audit Office was still reporting shortcomings. It estimated that hospitals recovered around half the amounts charged directly to patients, mainly visitors from outside the European Economic Area. [2]

The government introduced the immigration health surcharge and allowed higher charges for certain patients. These changes raised revenue. But the NAO found that much of the increase followed changes to charging rules, rather than demonstrating that hospitals had solved their identification problems. [2]

Research should lead to action. When the same weaknesses persist for years, publishing another report becomes a poor substitute for competent government.

£234 million written off in six Conservative years

The final six complete financial years before Labour took office provide a damning record:

These are recorded write-offs in official accounts and parliamentary answers. [4][5][6]

£234 million during six years of Conservative government.

The party that lectures Britain about financial responsibility should explain that record. Its ministers had the warnings. They had the authority. They had the time.

Taxpayers are entitled to judge the results.

Labour now owns the responsibility

Another £58 million was written off in 2024/25, the financial year spanning the change of government. It covers both administrations, and write-offs can concern bills from earlier years. [6][20]

Labour inherited the problem. It also inherited responsibility for addressing it.

Yet in February 2025, Labour’s health minister told Parliament that maternity write-offs were not held centrally and that there were no plans to estimate them. [7]

Why not?

How are taxpayers supposed to judge improvement when ministers cannot readily provide that national picture?

Labour cannot spend its term pointing backwards. The public needs evidence that hospitals are identifying chargeable patients and collecting more of what they are owed.

What those millions mean for patients

These bills represent clinical time, beds, medicines, tests and treatment. The care has been delivered. The expected payment has not been recovered.

The Government’s published average cost for a planned procedure in 2023/24 was £751, across outpatient procedures, day cases and elective inpatient care.

The £44 million written off that year was equivalent in value to approximately 58,600 planned procedures. That is a comparison of financial scale, not a count of cancelled operations. [6][11]

For patients waiting in pain, the value of hospital resources is anything but abstract.

A service struggling to provide timely treatment cannot afford complacency about legitimate charges going unpaid.

The recorded debt leaves some costs unseen

An unpaid invoice can be counted. A charge that was never raised cannot appear in the write-off total.

The Government’s 2012 charging review cited estimates of around 500,000 undocumented migrants. It acknowledged difficulties measuring evasion of identification and charging.

That historical estimate is not a current headcount, and exemptions mean immigration status alone does not determine whether every service is chargeable. [10]

The important finding is the administrative gap: recorded debts cannot capture all chargeable treatment that escaped billing.

The 2013 research reinforced this concern. Staff acknowledged that hospitals were failing to identify all chargeable patients. [9]

The full value of missed charging remains uncertain. That should trouble ministers, rather than excuse inaction.

When collection fails, taxpayers get another demand

Successive governments have proved far more decisive about increasing National Insurance than securing reliable collection of overseas-patient charges.

Under Boris Johnson, the Conservatives introduced a 1.25 percentage-point National Insurance increase in April 2022 to fund health and social care. It applied to employees, employers and the self-employed.

The increase was reversed that November. The separate Health and Social Care Levy planned for April 2023 was cancelled before it began. The government said the additional health and care funding would be maintained. [13]

A tax increase, a reversal and another funding promise—while overseas-patient debts continued to be written off.

Labour then increased the main employer National Insurance rate from 13.8% to 15% and lowered the annual earnings threshold at which employers start paying from £9,100 to £5,000, effective from April 2025.

Employers were charged a higher rate, starting at a much lower level of earnings. The Government explicitly linked the increase to funding the NHS and wider public services. [14]

Successive governments failed to collect legitimate NHS charges. Their answer to wider funding pressures included demanding more money from British employers.

Recovering overseas debts would not replace the billions raised through National Insurance. It would demonstrate that government takes protecting existing resources seriously.

Calling it an employer tax does not insulate workers from its effects. The Government’s own assessment acknowledged that higher employment costs would reduce wages and profits and could increase consumer prices. [14]

Workers and businesses face the pressure

The latest ONS figures show 92,000 fewer payrolled employees in June–August 2026 than a year earlier.

Vacancies fell to 691,000 in July–September, down 37,000 over the year. Outside the pandemic period, vacancies had not been this low since 2014. The ONS reported feedback suggesting higher labour costs were discouraging recruitment among smaller firms. [15]

Business distress remains substantial. 1,882 companies entered insolvency in England and Wales in September 2026, with approximately one in 200 companies entering insolvency over the preceding year. Although down on the previous year, that still represents serious financial distress. [16]

These are national economic figures, not a tally of losses caused solely by National Insurance. They show the environment in which ministers chose to increase employment costs.

Government should be relentless about collecting money owed before treating businesses and workers as the dependable source of another funding increase.

Patients face consequences beyond money

The National Audit Office reported in September 2026 that the proportion of patients spending at least 12 hours in A&E had tripled since before the pandemic.

It cited ONS analysis finding that patients waiting 12 hours were twice as likely to die within 30 days of leaving A&E as those waiting two hours. This is an association, not a calculation of deaths caused by unpaid overseas bills. [12]

Long waits are a patient-safety issue.

The same NAO report identified high bed occupancy, hospital bottlenecks and delayed discharge as important pressures. NHS failure has multiple causes; overseas debt is one documented financial failure within that wider picture. [12]

Patients deserve timely care. Taxpayers deserve competent stewardship. Neither should have to accept repeated warnings followed by years of inadequate results.

Reform proposes collecting more upfront

Reform UK proposes keeping the NHS tax-funded and free at the point of use for British citizens, while requiring foreign nationals covered by its surcharge policy to contribute more towards access. Its published position allows continued NHS access through a higher health surcharge. [17][18]

In November 2025, Reform proposed increasing the annual immigration health surcharge from £1,035 to £2,718, projecting £5 billion a year in revenue. That is the party’s forecast. [19]

The principle is straightforward: collect a larger contribution before treatment is needed.

The surcharge already exists. Reform proposes increasing it substantially. Hospitals would still need effective checks and collection procedures for chargeable visitors outside that system.

The Conservatives had years to strengthen those systems. Labour now has responsibility for making them work. Neither should escape scrutiny by reaching for another demand on British taxpayers.

Reform’s proposals should face the practical test both established parties have failed to satisfy: how much money is actually collected, and does the system protect frontline care?

Stop announcing intentions. Publish results.

Hospitals must provide immediately necessary care, including maternity treatment, as required. They must also establish entitlement accurately, apply exemptions correctly and recover legitimate charges.

The public deserves comparable annual figures showing what was billed, collected, left outstanding and written off.

It deserves accountability when collection systems fail. Above all, it deserves governments that treat warnings as instructions to act.

The Conservatives cannot talk their way out of their record.

Labour cannot inherit the machinery of government and disclaim responsibility for making it work.

Both parties demand public confidence in their stewardship of the NHS. Hundreds of millions in written-off bills give taxpayers every reason to demand better.

Figures & methodology

Scope: NHS providers in England. These are overseas-patient losses/write-offs across verified financial years, not a maternity-only total or an exact total for either government’s term. The category includes foreign nationals and British nationals living abroad; the combined sum is not exclusively debt owed by foreigners.

Calculation: £409,312,297, rounded to approximately £409 million, by adding the entries below. Most later source figures are themselves rounded to millions. The financial year 2012/13 is excluded because its comparable write-off total has not been verified in this investigation. No unverified estimate has been substituted.

Show the full annual calculation
Verified entries used in the combined figure
YearRecorded losses/write-offs
2010/11£13,955,733
2011/12£11,556,564
2013/14£15,200,000
2014/15£16,900,000
2015/16£15,700,000
2016/17£17,000,000
2017/18£27,000,000
2018/19£30,000,000
2019/20£41,000,000
2020/21£46,000,000
2021/22£36,000,000
2022/23£37,000,000
2023/24£44,000,000
2024/25£58,000,000
Combined sum£409,312,297

Timing: A write-off in a financial year may concern earlier treatment. The 2010/11 year includes weeks before the Conservatives entered office; 2024/25 spans both governments. Outstanding invoices, impairment provisions and write-offs are different measures and have not been added together. Accounting write-off does not necessarily cancel the legal debt.

Comparisons: £44,000,000 ÷ £751 ≈ 58,600 planned procedures. This is an illustration of financial scale, not a count of lost operations or unique patients. Labour-market and insolvency statistics are not attributed solely to National Insurance. A&E mortality associations are not evidence of deaths caused by unpaid overseas-patient bills.

Policy: Reform’s surcharge and revenue numbers are attributed proposals, announced in November 2025, not achieved revenues. Historical population estimates are not presented as current counts. The hospital illustration is AI-generated and depicts no identified hospital incident.
